Nobody ever told you this…

But knowing your rules and following them are two different skills.

Most traders get the first one down early. The second takes years.

You say you’ll risk the same amount every trade. Then one looks “different” and you size up.

You say you’ll wait for your level. Price runs and you jump in so you don’t miss it.

You take a loss and want it back right now.

You say you’re done for the day. Then you open one more chart.

I’ve lost $800k averaging down on $NQ. I’ve lived this one.

More videos, more notes, more studying won’t fix it. Practice will, and it has to happen when it’s uncomfortable.

Here’s what helped me:

Grade every trade on whether you followed your plan. Ignore whether it made money.

Count your rule breaks each week. Watch that number.

Give yourself credit for sitting out. It’s a trade too.

Never average down on a losing position. Desperation will end you.

Protect your capital first.

Every rule you bend gets easier to bend. Every rule you keep gets easier to keep.

Build the habit first. The money comes after.

posts.text:
$MRVL has lost about 50% of its value in one month. 

Today CEO Matt Murphy emailed every employee to explain it, under the subject line "Putting the Week in Perspective."

What happened, in his words:

1. Last week Marvell agreed to combine with $LITE. Murphy says "some of the initial analyst commentary and media coverage reflected a misunderstanding of the strategic rationale."

2. The large shareholders he met in Boston and New York "told a very different story." He says they understood the case for joining silicon and optics, and recognized Marvell's acquisition track record.

3. Their most common question was "why now?" His answer points to Inphi, which put Marvell ahead of the move to scale-out optics. Optics are now moving into scale-up and scale-in, and "customers are making important technology decisions now that will shape the next generation of AI infrastructure."

4. On the stock, he gives the number plainly. "Marvell shares declined approximately 51%, closely in line with the 49% average decline among our connectivity peers." $LITE saw a similar decline.

5. He ties that to a selloff across AI stocks. Part of the cause is "uncertainty about how long the current AI infrastructure investment cycle will continue." He adds that the midterms "brought increased attention" to data center expansion and "the possibility of additional restrictions."

6. His counterpoint is the longer window. "Marvell shares are still up approximately 66% year to date," ahead of both connectivity and broader AI peers, and he says the long-term trends behind AI infrastructure spending "remain strong."

7. He ends by telling staff the deal alone won't pay off. "Simply acquiring a company doesn't create value. It's what we do afterward." That part is still far off, because the deal isn't expected to close until the first half of 2028 and the two companies stay independent until then.

The Senate voted 73-25 Monday to advance the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act. Trump has endorsed it, and more votes are expected this week.

The bill speeds up federal approvals for power plants and power lines, and it makes large data centers pay for the grid upgrades built to serve them, so those costs don’t land on regular electric customers.

I think the bill favors data centers that use behind the meter power generation, for two reasons.

On cost, Grid Strategies estimates data centers would pay about $55B in transmission charges over ten years under the bill, against roughly $20B at current rates.

On time, the median wait for a grid connection is already more than five years, per Berkeley Lab, while permitting a gas plant on site takes 6 to 18 months before construction starts.

Google’s $GOOG Wyoming campus shows what that looks like in practice. $AEP is building a 702 MW plant of Bloom Energy $BE fuel cells outside its regulated utility territory, and Google’s 20 year contract for the output pays for it, so no Wyoming household pays toward it.

quoted.text:
The Data Center Buildout Is Not Dead

The Senate’s 73-25 vote to advance the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act undercuts the claim that rapid data center expansion is politically finished. 

With White House support and President Trump publicly backing the measure as a way to unleash energy production and protect ratepayers, the bill both raises costs for operators and clears the largest practical obstacle to new capacity: the inability to build power and transmission on a workable timeline.

Under the legislation, large loads of roughly 20 megawatts or more must cover the full incremental cost of the generation, transmission, and distribution upgrades built to serve them. Ratepayers are shielded from cost shifting, and states gain additional tools to impose collateral or other requirements. Modeling suggests this could meaningfully increase the retail power price faced by data centers and add roughly 10 percent to the annualized cost of a gigawatt-scale facility. Those numbers are real, and some marginal projects will be repriced or delayed.

They are not fatal. The same bill shortens federal environmental reviews, limits the window for legal challenges, strengthens project certainty, and expands federal transmission siting authority after a defined state review period. posts.text:
Pg 2 of 2.  $NVDA FT article 11/10/2026

For Nvidia’s shareholders, being rid of Huang would have some virtues. If he stays, uncertainty about the company’s future could feed on itself as more information dribbles out and investigations drag on.

Nvidia will face increased oversight and potentially regulation, including through stricter controls on the chips it is allowed to export and to whom. The CEO and his team will be distracted from their core responsibilities. He can only emerge with his industry stature diminished. No longer will he be a trusted confidant of politicians or an intermediary in geopolitically sensitive trade deals. 

This is about revenue, not just reputation. Three congressional committees have requested that Huang appear before them, and formal inquiries could follow. 

The argument that Huang should stay is worth hearing too. Huang built Nvidia into one of the world’s most valuable companies and it has done astonishingly well for investors. Its shares have risen nearly thirteenfold since the launch of ChatGPT in 2022. His boldness, and underwriting of the AI build-out by investing directly in companies that could become major customers for Nvidia’s chips, has been central to its success. Replacing him now would mean losing one of the AI boom’s visionaries and an important counterweight to the sometimes apocalyptic visions of the model makers Altman and Amodei.

It’s also not clear that anyone at Nvidia is ready to succeed Huang. A hasty replacement could be a disaster for the company and the industry. The culture of the organisation has been built around Huang and his preference for a flat organisational structure. He has several dozen direct reports. The chair-less board is dominated by longstanding professional associates of his, and it’s possible they are simply unprepared (and yes, that’s a sackable offence, too).

If a company cannot function without its founder, that’s an indictment of its business model and its culture. Imperial CEOs are bad for companies and for capitalism. But removing Huang may simply be too big a risk. There are no good outcomes here.

posts.name: Gary Black
posts.text:
To me this is not about $NVDA CEO Jensen Huang’s affair with Chinese executive Alice Huang.   It’s about whether he misled NVDA’s board about his involvement and potential conflict of interest with a major and geopolitically sensitive customer?  And did he use his stature as NVDA’s CEO to circumvent the U.S. ban on selling chips to China? 

There’s no question that Jensen Huang is one of the greatest CEOs of our time, and $NVDA is worth far more with him than without him. When it comes to the board of directors’ decision to remove or not remove him to preserve the long term value of the firm, that is unfortunately not relevant.

NVDA’s Nvidia’s Dilemma:  Will Jensen Huang Remain as CEO of $NVDA? Should He?
Financial Times - 11/10/2026

There is a lot the world is still to discover about the affair Huang has admitted to having. US officials suspect him of a relationship with Alice Huang, who they believe was spying for China. She was a Chinese executive at Megaspeed International. The Singapore-based cloud computing provider is a customer of Nvidia and, according to Megaspeed’s company documents, has been the recipient of loans from the US chip group in 2024. 
It has also been the subject of a US investigation over concerns it was smuggling Nvidia’s chips into China. The company has denied allegations of any illicit activity involving chips. 

Given just these basic facts, and given the acute geopolitical sensitivity of the advanced semiconductor industry, we know for certain that Mr Huang has demonstrated bad judgment on an epic scale — even before the allegation that Ms Huang is a spy for China’s Ministry of State Security is considered. What happens next is very important for Nvidia’s investors, customers and competitors. It is also a referendum on the accountability of leaders of the megacap tech companies whose influence on the world stage is greater than that of most nations.

Here are the key facts we know:

Nvidia is the indispensable supplier and, increasingly, financier of the infrastructure powering the entire AI boom;
 Huang is the boom’s chief salesperson and its most influential figure who is not running one of the AI labs; Huang is a trusted adviser to Donald Trump on the US-China AI race and AI regulation;
 US intelligence has believed for months that Huang had a romantic relationship with Alice Huang.

Here’s some of what we don’t know:

Did Huang mislead Nvidia’s board? Did he disclose that he had a conflict of interest with a major and geopolitically sensitive customer? Did the board know US intelligence suspected Alice Huang of being linked to Chinese intelligence?
 Did the company know about the affair when it told The New York Times two weeks ago that the relationship was “not unusual or unexpected” for the executive of an important commercial partner?
 How strong is the evidence that has led US intelligence to conclude that Alice Huang is a spy?

We’ll leave the political story to others. Our turf is whether Huang can continue in his role and what that means for investors.

The argument that he should go starts with his failure of judgment. The problem is not infidelity, but rather gross disregard for security and political risk at a pivotal moment for the industry. On our count, there are barely a handful of CEOs who could make such disclosures and still be in post the next day — Elon Musk, Mark Zuckerberg, Sam Altman and, perhaps soon, Dario Amodei. One cannot help but wonder whether the identification of Jensen Huang with his company, and his aura of indispensability, contributed to the collapse of his judgment. 

Certainly it highlights the risks associated with imperial CEOs. Allowing Huang to remain in his job, even with a more rigorous management and governance structure around him, compounds the original sin — impunity.

📺 HOT CPI JUST GAVE ME ANOTHER REASON NOT TO TRUST THIS BOUNCE + $SPY / $QQQ KEY LEVELS  + BLOOD IN THE STREET ACCOUNT UPDATE #2 + WHY I DON’T TRUST ANALYSTS + $TSLA LOOK

The market has gone from extremely oversold on Thursday last week to neutral after a powerful rebound.

But does that mean the correction is over? Not necessarily.

We've been stuck in a frustrating, range-bound market since July, and one strong bounce doesn't change that.

*

Now CPI has come in hotter than expected.

Headline inflation rose 0.4% month-over-month versus 0.3% expected, while core CPI increased 0.3% versus 0.2% expected.

That creates another obstacle for a market already struggling with broken leadership and major technical resistance.

*

$SPY rallied from roughly $733 to $755, pushing straight through the $749–$750 area I was watching.

That's a 22-point move for anyone who bought the weakness. Many traders took profits on most of their positions, which makes sense for a trading account.

*

But my BOS Account is different.

It's a long-term strategy, not a swing trade. With the market only about 6% off its highs when I bought, I deployed 25% of the account.

I'm not selling that position after a quick bounce. The plan is to hold for a recovery toward new all-time highs.

*

Now comes the real test.  With CPI hot, we could retrace part of this rally.

The question is whether buyers defend support or whether this becomes another broken bounce.

If $SPY pushes toward the upper end of its range, I'd rather evaluate a fade at resistance than chase an extended move.

*

$QQQ also faces a critical technical test around its moving averages, including the 200-day.

A rebound is one thing but reclaiming and holding those levels is another.

*

Meanwhile, $IWM was showing relative strength, with $276.86 as an important support reference. That's encouraging, but the major growth leaders still aren't leading.

*

Lower oil prices have helped the tape.

$USO broke down after a failed breakout and remains under pressure, while $TLT near $82 could become constructive if it breaks higher and longer-term yields decline.

*

And here's why I don't trust Wall Street analysts.

Bank of America is reportedly removing $NVDA, $MU and $LRCX from its top buy list after substantial weakness.

Where were these downgrades when everyone was bullish near the highs? Analysts raise targets after stocks run and cut them after they've already collapsed.

I trust charts, price action and reactions to news far more than price targets, so should you.

*

As for $TSLA, it's another range-bound, broken trade.

Watch yesterday's high at $382.20. A move above that level could create an opportunity, but sustained follow-through remains the challenge.

*

So, the bounce was powerful, but hot CPI, damaged growth leadership and major resistance levels leave plenty of reasons to stay cautious.

Whether the market can sustain a rally into year-end remains uncertain.

Know your levels, don't chase, and let price action tell you what comes next.

It has been a crazy week, and indeed a fairly tumultuous couple of months, as markets have had to reevaluate evolving AI-related stories, election results and geopolitical developments, and for a time inflation had been pushed to the side as a real-time relevant news story. That being said, to the Federal Reserve this inflation story is top of mind, particularly as last week's employment report showed a still solid no-hire/no-fire labor market. With today's stronger-than-expected inflation print, a Fed policy rate hike in December appears quite likely and the question is more about whether it will be a quarter point hike or a half point.

The headline CPI print of 0.35% month-over-month remained quite elevated, in part due to increases in energy and food costs, and Core CPI, while a bit more subdued at 0.30% month-over-month, was still well above the Fed's 2% target. The 3-month and 6-month annualized moving averages of Core CPI reside at 3.75% and 2.70%, respectively, displaying price gains that continue to be considerably higher than the Fed is comfortable with.

Despite some technical uncertainty, higher than desired levels of inflation should keep the Fed dissatisfied with the lackluster progress on inflation. When dissecting today's number further, core goods ex-autos inflation accelerated to 0.5% month-over-month and supercore edged up to 0.4% month-over-month. We, and the Fed, will continue to watch these numbers as they evolve over the coming months.

The Fed's disposition, as well as that of many global central banks today, is to keep policy firm to try to address these elevated inflationary conditions. We understand the directive here, but think that in many places, such as the U.S., it is very hard to address exogenous near-term shocks, such as fuel prices influenced by geopolitical developments, or semiconductor prices influenced by a memory/compute shortage as the AI buildout rages on, via conventional policymaking. These sorts of shocks are only very loosely tied to the overnight interest rate tool as a moderator of these conditions.

Hence, we maintain a cautious stance with regard to interest rates, in anticipation of potentially higher rates from here, but also respectful of the chances for easing geopolitical tensions and some potentially slower AI investment over the coming quarters and years, alleviating some of this near-term pricing pressure in the technology space. Still, we remain resolute in our posture that income remains at the forefront of investment decisions for fixed income portfolios. The availability here is generationally attractive and continues to provide greater stability than more volatile interest rate expressions. Further, patient investors continue to be rewarded for clipping coupon, especially when both stock prices and general price levels in these recurring inflation reports are displaying meaningful volatility.

Fed Governor Christopher Waller put a 50-basis-point hike on the table for December if US core #inflation came in at around 0.3% or higher. It came in at 0.3%, above the 0.2% economists expected.

The US is an “overfinancialized” economy, meaning that higher interest rates, lower liquidity, and falling equity prices have a disproportionate effect on economic activity and market sentiment.

Inflation has been above the Fed’s target for years. That sets up a potentially epic standoff.

Accept higher yields and tighter financial conditions, and the debt-driven economy could take a hit. Equities and other risk assets could plummet.

Distort bond markets by pushing down interest rates, and you risk fueling inflation and eroding the purchasing power of dollars, savings, and fixed payments on government debt.

In the first scenario, hold something outside the financial system. In the second scenario, hold something that protects purchasing power.

If it were me, I would have built the CyberSUV and tried to see what demand was for that. If that had not meaningfully improved line utilization, then I would have dismantled the line for more Cybercab capacity.

Cybertruck owners/fans are a very passionate group, and rightfully so, it's legit an incredible vehicle, but it generates ~$2B a year in revenue (vs $20B for Model 3 and $50B for Model Y) and likely very little profit.

Cybertruck will make up less than 2% of Tesla's revenue in 2026, so I can understand why Elon would look at that factory square footage and come to the conclusion that Tesla could make 25-50x more revenue in that space with Cybercab, and thus want to dismantle the line.

I hope Tesla continues to invest in personally owned vehicles, because a lot of people will continue to want to own their own vehicle (especially in America) for specific scenarios (large families riding together, luggage, etc). This is what sequence of return risk looks like. What mitigates this? Diversification across time and assets. 

Asset liability matching strategies like Defined Duration ALM compartmentalize your allocation by time horizon and assets to mitigate sequence risk knowing that equities are long duration assets (15+ years) that cannot reliably fund short-term liabilities.

So what do you do? You own shorter duration assets (or insurance like instruments). 

Global 60/40, which is typically a 10-15 year type instrument, was up 80% during this period. 

US 60/40 was up 75%. 

5 year treasuries were up 110%. 

Tbills were up 28%. 

You see - you can systematically match these assets by time horizon to reduce the duration risk imposed by long duration instruments like stocks. 

If you add insurance instruments - gold was up 519%, managed futures were up 110%. 

This is how you mitigate sequence risk. You diversify across time AND assets.

Tesla has submitted a new letter to NHTSA, urging the federal government to modernize U.S. vehicle lighting regulations.

Tesla argues that existing regulations were designed for traditional headlights, not modern matrix LED systems that use vehicle cameras to detect other vehicles, pedestrians, and cyclists and dynamically adjust light beams to improve visibility and reduce glare.

Tesla also wants regulations to account for lighting improvements delivered through over-the-air software updates and is pushing for automakers to have greater representation in shaping the new rules.

Semiautomatic beam switching and adaptive driving beam functions are therefore scene understanding problems, not binary light-threshold problems.

Tesla has concerns about NHTSA’s proposed composition of the advisory committee tasked with reaching consensus recommendations. Specifically, Tesla urges the agency to increase the number of individual vehicle manufacturer committee members from the current proposal of just two representatives. Power constraints and interconnection queues were already going to push some projects later. Politics is now an additional variable, not the sole driver.

You have no idea what you're talking about - starting with low limits in order to build credit is exactly how the industry already works.

Credit cards are unsecured debt on a REVOLVER: the cardholder has the ability to draw down credit at the moment that is most advantageous to them but most dangerous for the lender (e.g., right after the borrower loses their job or has a massive incident (car repair, healthcare issue, etc.)). By its nature, it is a very dangerous loan to offer.

Further, unlike home mortgages or car loans, credit card loans are unsecured (ie, there is no asset to foreclose on in a default), so recovery rates in default are very low, leading to very high losses.

The risk to the lender is extreme, and interest compensates for that risk.

Keep in mind that the card companies (mostly banks) finance these loans, and that the cost of funds is SOFR+. They also have operating costs, servicing costs, etc.

Imagine a world where Fed Funds or SOFR itself is 10%; the idea of a fixed 10% cap on interest rates is intellectually disqualifying for anyone who proposes it.

quoted.text:
INFLATION IS STILL A MONETARY PHENOMENON

I have looked at 42 countries since December 2019. For each one I compared how much faster broad money has grown than the real economy with how high inflation has been.

The slope is 0.50 – one percentage point more money growth a year has meant roughly half a percentage point more inflation.

R² is 0.57 – differences in money growth explain 57% of the differences in inflation across countries.

The countries that printed the most money got the most inflation. Switzerland and Japan, where money barely outgrew the economy, got the least.

The US sits just above the line. The euro area sits almost on it.

So forget supply chain disruptions and greedflation – that was always nonsense. Supply shocks change relative prices. They do not create years of broad-based inflation across 42 countries.

It is money, and it still is. Nominal spending remains excessive across the world, and that is what is keeping inflation elevated everywhere.

The ECB’s French Dilemma: Buying Time Is Not Buying Solvency

France’s sovereign risk increasingly reflects three interconnected vulnerabilities: geopolitical exposure, fiscal deterioration and dependence on the ECB. 
Falling oil prices ease inflationary pressures and support French bonds. But lower yields should not be confused with restored fiscal credibility. Markets may simply be unwinding a geopolitical risk premium rather than reassessing France’s debt sustainability.
As Desmond Lachman recently warned, the ECB could face a difficult choice between containing sovereign debt contagion and compromising its own eligibility rules and institutional credibility.
The deeper paradox is that cheaper oil may postpone the ECB’s dilemma without resolving France’s structural weaknesses.
The real test will come when oil prices stabilise: will investors continue financing France without credible fiscal reforms or the implicit protection of the ECB?
Ultimately, the eurozone’s resilience cannot rest indefinitely on monetary intervention compensating for national fiscal dysfunction. Lower oil prices buy France time—but only political action can turn that time into lasting credibility.

🔥No official U.S. CPI YoY number today — but we can still estimate it.

Because of the 2025 government shutdown, BLS never collected October 2025 CPI data, leaving it unable to calculate the usual year-over-year comparison for today’s release.

We backfilled the missing October 2025 observations with Bloomberg-derived estimates. On that basis, headline CPI is running at roughly 4.02% YoY in October, up from 3.74% in September.

The contribution breakdown is also notable:

• Core services: +2.06 percentage points
• Energy: +1.33 pp
• Food: +0.41 pp
• Core goods: +0.19 pp
That comes alongside the official October monthly readings of +0.4% headline and +0.3% core, both above consensus.

Methodology: Missing September 2025 weights are estimated by updating December 2024 weights for subsequent price changes, with the same weights used for October. Missing October 2025 index values are estimated as the geometric mean of September and November 2025.

These are Bloomberg-derived estimates, not official BLS figures.

I'm always in admiration of @Ritholtz for the way he unpacks things. In particular, I think his capturing of leverage in the system -- both ETFs and hedge funds -- is elegant. 

If this were 1998 and HFs faced this type of carnage, there would have been much larger ripples, and the banking system would have felt it too. Instead, we got a garden variety deleveraging. Why is this? 

The modern behavior of a pod shop. 

If you're losing money quickly, you're stopped out. There's little shot at redemption. The risk management functions within many of these multi-strats have not only worked pretty remarkably, they've also contained contained the damage such that banks did not face meaningful issues tied to the selloffs. 

Barry's best point? There exists a market structure that absorbs -- and even benefits -- from such shocks. Someone won on November 5.
